title: Multiplayer agentic engineering — Arjun Singh, Superconductor

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk's core is about structuring agent systems for collaborative, multi-interface, model-agnostic team workflows. The six lessons define a comprehensive agent control plane and harness architecture: shared sessions reachable from Slack/desktop/GitHub, model and harness agnosticism as a design principle, collaborative visibility, external signal ingestion into agent workflows, and isolation as an architectural constraint. While coding agents are the application, the primary focus is the harness architecture and how agents integrate into team workflows.

secondary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
secondary.rationale: The entire workflow centers on coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) generating PRs, with ~99.9% of pull requests heavily agent-generated. Custom benchmarking replays representative PRs, SWE-bench is explicitly discussed as a comparison point, and the practical application domain is software engineering with agents writing and shipping code.

secondary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance
secondary.rationale: Lesson four dedicates significant depth to least-privilege security, network sandboxes blocking exfiltration of code and secrets, per-ticket and per-project endpoint grants, and the concrete risk of agents finding production tokens on developer machines. Security governance is a core architectural pillar of the system.

secondary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
secondary.rationale: Lesson five details a custom benchmarking methodology: selecting representative PRs, replaying them across harnesses, and plotting quality vs cost and time. The talk argues against public benchmarks in favor of codebase-specific evaluation, and mentions future automatic model routing based on these benchmarks.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Superconductor builds a platform for agentic engineering used by software builders. The talk describes infrastructure for agent sessions, sandboxes, benchmarking dashboards, and integrations that other engineering teams build on.

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: The agents are coding assistants generating PRs, prototyping features from meeting transcripts, and reviewing code. Claude Code and Codex are the primary harnesses, and the output is software engineering work.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: Meeting bot ingestion from Google Meet, Slack integration for non-technical team members, and customer call processing represent enterprise workflow automation turning operational signals into engineering work.

summary: Arjun Singh, co-founder and CEO of Superconductor, presents "Multiplayer agentic engineering" at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. His team, together for over a decade and formerly at Gradescope (acquired by Turnitin in 2018), built a platform integrating AI coding agents into team workflows. He presents six lessons (indexed from zero): (0) Be model and harness agnostic—the best option changes weekly, open-weight models like GLM 5.2 are now viable and cheaper, and token vendors' incentives diverge from yours. (1) Turn every human interface into a shared agent-human interface—one session reachable from Slack, desktop app, and GitHub with full context preserved. (2) Make agent work visible and collaborative—teammates can see who is involved, ask the agent questions in-thread, and view artifacts from anywhere. (3) Turn every external signal—Slack, customer calls, Sentry alerts—into code automatically; a meeting bot demo shows it autonomously creating tickets and prototyping changes from overheard conversation during a four-hour Google Meet. (4) Run all work in an isolated cloud environment with configurable network sandboxes for least-privilege security—an agent told to wipe staging could find production tokens on a developer's laptop and cause catastrophic damage. (5) Benchmark agents on your own codebase—SWE-bench is Python and they use Ruby on Rails; they replay representative PRs and plot quality vs cost and time. Results over one month: approximately 99.9% of PRs are heavily agent-generated (all human-reviewed), with Codex outperforming Claude on cost while running four times as many sessions. He closes with three recommendations: get your codebase working in a sandbox, integrate agents into human interfaces, and benchmark to stay model-agnostic.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form an integrated architecture for team-scale agentic engineering. The SE concepts—multi-interface sessions, model agnosticism, custom benchmarking, network sandboxing, least-privilege security, and cloud isolation—define the infrastructure layer that makes agents safe, switchable, and measurable. The AI concepts—multiplayer agentic engineering, open-weight model viability, coding agent harnesses, autonomous meeting bots, and token economics—define the intelligence and application layer that drives productivity. Together, they address the talk's central thesis: agents are powerful but must be embedded in human workflows with security, visibility, and evaluation tailored to the team's codebase. The security concepts (least privilege, network sandboxing, exfiltration prevention) enable the collaboration concepts (multi-interface sessions, non-technical triggering) by providing the trust boundary that makes broad access safe. The benchmarking concepts (codebase-specific evaluation, quality-vs-cost-vs-time) enable model agnosticism by providing the data to make switching decisions rationally. The talk's production metrics (99.9% agent-generated PRs, billions of tokens, Codex outperforming Claude on cost) demonstrate that this integrated architecture is not theoretical but operational at production scale.
temporalContext: The talk was presented at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 (video published August 9, 2026), with research conducted as of August 23, 2026. GLM-5.2 was released June 16, 2026, approximately two months before the talk. The SWE-bench benchmark paper was published at ICLR 2024. Superconductor was founded in 2025 with $7M in funding, and their engineering blog posts date from July 2025 (why-we-built) and October 2025 (agent-benchmarks). The team's decade-long collaboration predates their current venture, having co-founded Gradescope (acquired by Turnitin in 2018). The production metrics cited (billions of tokens, 3,300 Claude Code runs) reflect approximately one month of operation preceding the talk.
takeaways: Be model and harness agnostic: the best option changes weekly, open-weight models are viable and cheaper, and token sellers' incentives are not aligned with your goals
One agent session should be reachable from Slack, desktop app, and GitHub simultaneously with full context preserved across all surfaces
Making agent work visible lets teammates ask the agent questions in-thread instead of waiting for the original author to respond
The meeting bot autonomously picks ideas from conversations, creates tickets, prototypes work, and produces screenshots without manual routing between systems
The real reason for isolated cloud environments is least-privilege security—an eager agent could find a production token on a developer's machine and accidentally delete production data

A configurable network sandbox blocks exfiltration and prompts before accessing new endpoints, grantable per ticket or project, enabling non-technical team members to safely trigger real engineering work
Benchmark agents on your own codebase rather than public benchmarks—SWE bench is Python and results differ significantly for Ruby on Rails codebases
Model agnosticism lets you switch defaults overnight when a new model launches with zero meaningful disruption to workflows
Over one month: 10.5 billion tokens, 3,300 Claude Code runs (~$10,000 token value), Codex running 4x as many sessions for less money, with ~99.9% of PRs agent-generated but all human-reviewed

concepts.name: Multiplayer agentic engineering
concepts.explanation: A paradigm for integrating AI agents into team workflows where multiple humans collaborate with agents through shared sessions, making agent work visible and collaborative rather than isolated on individual machines.
concepts.importance: Represents a shift from single-user agent interactions to team-scale agent orchestration, addressing the gap between agent capabilities and human collaboration patterns that most talks overlook.

concepts.name: Open-weight models as coding agent alternatives
concepts.explanation: Open-weight models like GLM 5.2 are now viable and cheaper alternatives to frontier API models for coding agent tasks, giving teams cost-effective options and reducing dependency on proprietary APIs.
concepts.importance: Expands the model landscape for coding agents beyond frontier APIs, enabling cost optimization and model-agnostic architectures. Externally verified: GLM-5.2 is a 744B-parameter MoE model with MIT license released June 16, 2026.

concepts.name: Coding agent harnesses with distinct cost-quality-speed profiles
concepts.explanation: Different coding agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex) exhibit distinct tradeoffs: Anthropic agents consistently improve in quality but at higher cost and slower speed, while Codex was faster, cheaper, and ran four times as many sessions.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that model selection should be data-driven and codebase-specific, as different harnesses optimize differently across quality, cost, and speed dimensions.

concepts.name: Autonomous meeting bot for software engineering
concepts.explanation: A bot that joins meetings (e.g., a four-hour Google Meet), autonomously extracts ideas from conversation, creates tickets, prototypes code changes, and produces screenshots without manual intervention.
concepts.importance: Shows a concrete application of LLMs bridging unstructured communication and structured engineering output, turning conversations into actionable code prototypes.

concepts.name: Automatic model routing based on codebase benchmarks
concepts.explanation: A future capability where the system automatically selects the best agent based on codebase-specific benchmark results, rather than relying on third-party routing decisions or manual model selection.
concepts.importance: Could eliminate the anxiety of trying every new model manually and optimize cost-quality-speed tradeoffs automatically per task, tailored to the team's specific codebase.

concepts.name: SWE-bench and its language-specificity limitation
concepts.explanation: SWE-bench is a widely-used public benchmark for evaluating LLMs on software engineering tasks, but its original version consists of 2,294 instances from 12 Python repositories, making it unsuitable for non-Python codebases like Ruby on Rails.
concepts.importance: Highlights the risk of relying on public benchmarks that do not reflect a team's technology stack, motivating codebase-specific evaluation. Externally verified via official website, GitHub repo, and ICLR 2024 paper.

concepts.name: Token economics for agent operations at scale
concepts.explanation: Managing large-scale token consumption—approximately 10.5 billion tokens over one month across 3,300 Claude Code runs worth approximately $10,000—with Codex running four times as many sessions for less money overall.
concepts.importance: Provides concrete production-scale data on the cost of running agent-driven engineering, informing budget and model selection decisions. Note: the exact token figure has a potential web disagreement (see disagreement note).

concepts.name: Agent exfiltration risk
concepts.explanation: The risk that an agent with broad network access could exfiltrate code, projects, secrets, or content to unauthorized external endpoints, necessitating configurable network sandboxes.
concepts.importance: A security threat model specific to autonomous agents that have access to sensitive codebases, requiring architectural controls beyond traditional application security.

concepts.name: Collaborative agent visibility
concepts.explanation: Making agent work visible and collaborative so team members can see who is involved in a session, ask the agent questions in-thread, and view artifacts like screenshots from any interface.
concepts.importance: Enables non-technical team members to participate in and review agent-driven engineering work, reducing bottlenecks on original authors and fostering team-wide trust in agent output.

concepts.name: Prototype-not-production agent output evaluation
concepts.explanation: Agent-generated changes from external signals are prototypes to evaluate, not final implementations; the speaker explicitly notes auto-generated acceptance-criteria changes probably will not ship as-is.
concepts.importance: Establishes the right expectation for agent-generated work from unstructured inputs, distinguishing ideation and prototyping from production-ready code.

concepts.name: Multi-interface agent session architecture
concepts.explanation: Designing agent sessions that are simultaneously reachable from Slack, desktop apps, and GitHub with full context preserved across all surfaces, eliminating the limitation of trapping agents on a single laptop or interface.
concepts.importance: Enables seamless collaboration where work can start, continue, and finish from different interfaces, which is essential for team-scale agent workflows.

concepts.name: Model and harness agnosticism
concepts.explanation: Architectural principle of not depending on a single LLM model or agent harness, enabling overnight switching when new models launch or availability changes, with zero meaningful workflow disruption.
concepts.importance: Protects team productivity when the best model changes weekly and prevents vendor lock-in, as token vendors' incentives to sell more tokens diverge from the team's goal of building a better product.

concepts.name: Custom codebase-specific benchmarking
concepts.explanation: Selecting representative pull requests from your own repository, replaying them across multiple agent harnesses, and plotting quality against cost and time rather than relying on public benchmarks like SWE-bench.
concepts.importance: Public benchmarks may not reflect a team's language or framework—SWE-bench is Python while Superconductor uses Ruby on Rails—so codebase-specific evaluation produces actionable, relevant comparisons.

concepts.name: Configurable network sandboxing for agents
concepts.explanation: A network sandbox that controls which external endpoints agents can access, with no-access, custom-access (default), and full-access modes, prompting for permission before accessing new endpoints and grantable per ticket or project.
concepts.importance: Prevents exfiltration of code, secrets, and content to unauthorized endpoints while allowing agents to access necessary dependencies, and enables non-technical team members to safely trigger real engineering work.

concepts.name: Least-privilege security for agents
concepts.explanation: Security principle restricting agent access to only what they need, motivated by the concrete risk that an agent told to wipe staging could find a production token on a developer's laptop and delete production data.
concepts.importance: Transforms agent security from convenience-based isolation to a principled access-control architecture, preventing catastrophic accidental damage from over-eager agents.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-loop code review for agent-generated PRs
concepts.explanation: Despite approximately 99.9% of pull requests being heavily agent-generated, all PRs remain human-reviewed before merging, maintaining quality control over autonomous code generation at production scale.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates a production-scale balance between agent autonomy and human oversight, showing that massive agent-generated code volume still requires human judgment for safety and quality.

concepts.name: External signal ingestion into engineering pipelines
concepts.explanation: Automatically turning signals from Slack, meetings, Sentry alerts, and emails into code and tickets, demonstrated by a meeting bot that autonomously created tickets from overheard conversation and prototyped code changes.
concepts.importance: Converts operational and communication data into actionable engineering work without manual routing, enabling every customer call to yield dozens of prototyped ideas and a few shippable PRs.

concepts.name: Isolated cloud development environments
concepts.explanation: Running all agent work in isolated cloud environments rather than on developer laptops, eliminating lid anxiety and enforcing security boundaries between agent access and production systems.
concepts.importance: Enables non-technical team members to trigger real engineering work without local development environments, while preventing agents from accessing developer machine secrets and tokens.

sections.title: Introduction and team background
sections.summary: Singh introduces himself and the talk's focus on people in agentic workflows. He shares the team's history: over a decade together, Berkeley PhD backgrounds, co-founding GradeScope, and now building Superconductor with aggressive agent integration over the past year.

sections.title: Lesson zero: Be model and harness agnostic
sections.summary: The best model and harness can change weekly due to new releases or availability changes. Open-weight models like GLM 5.2 are now good and cheaper. Token vendors' incentives to sell more tokens diverge from your goal of building a better product, so staying switchable keeps you in control.

sections.title: Lesson one: Turn every human interface into an agent and human interface
sections.summary: Agents trapped on a laptop are too narrow; Slack bots are better but still limiting. The goal is one agent session reachable from Slack, desktop app, and GitHub, with full context preserved across all surfaces so work can start, continue, and finish from different interfaces.

sections.title: Lesson two: Make agent work visible and collaborative
sections.summary: Team members should see who is involved in an agent session, ask the agent questions directly in-thread instead of waiting for the author, and view artifacts like screenshots from any interface. This matters especially when non-technical people trigger work that engineers need to vet.

sections.title: Lesson three: Turn every external signal into code
sections.summary: Signals from Slack, meetings, Sentry, emails, and bug reports should become code automatically. The meeting bot demo shows a four-hour Google Meet where the bot autonomously created tickets from overheard ideas—including one about coding agents needing acceptance criteria, which it prototyped and screenshotted. Singh clarifies these are prototypes to evaluate, not final implementations, but every call now yields dozens of ideas and a few shippable PRs.

sections.title: Lesson four: Isolated cloud environment with network sandbox
sections.summary: Running agents in an isolated cloud environment eliminates lid anxiety and, more importantly, enforces least privilege. An agent told to wipe staging could find a production token on a developer's laptop and delete everything. A configurable network sandbox blocks exfiltration of code, secrets, and content, prompting for permission when an agent tries to access a new endpoint—grantable per ticket or project. This isolation is what lets non-technical team members trigger real engineering work via Slack without development environments, because the sandbox handles security. An environment setup assistant helps get projects working in these sandboxes.

sections.title: Lesson five: Benchmark agents on your codebase
sections.summary: Public benchmarks like SWE bench may not reflect your work—SWE bench is Python and Superconductor is Ruby on Rails. They select representative pull requests, replay them across agents, and plot quality vs cost and quality vs time. Results showed Anthropic agents improving in quality but not speed and at higher cost, while Codex was faster and cheaper. They switched defaults to Codex, briefly to Fiable when it launched, then back to Codex when it went away—all with no meaningful disruption due to model agnosticism. Benchmarking also eliminates the anxiety of trying every new model manually and enables future automatic model routing tailored to their codebase.

sections.title: Recommendations and closing
sections.summary: Singh closes with three recommendations: get your codebase working in a sandbox, integrate agents into human interfaces so teams avoid context switching, and benchmark to become model-agnostic and stay on the frontier of cost, speed, and quality. Over one month their small team consumed 10.5 billion tokens across 3,300 Claude Code runs (~$10,000 token value) and Codex ran four times as many sessions for less money, with approximately 99.9% of PRs heavily agent-generated but all human-reviewed. He invites attendees to the expo booth and notes a MacBook Neo giveaway.

organization.name: Superconductor
organization.summary: Superconductor (superconductor.com) is a privately held US technology company founded in 2025, building a multiplayer workspace platform for software teams and AI coding agents. Founded by Arjun Singh (CEO), Sergey Karayev, and Kevin Gutowski—who previously co-founded Gradescope (acquired by Turnitin in 2018)—the company has 7 employees and is backed by $7M in funding. The platform enables teams to run multiple coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Factory Droid, Grok Build, Amp, Cursor) in shared cloud sessions accessible from Slack, GitHub, desktop, and mobile. Key features include cloud sandboxes with configurable network policies, a custom benchmarking dashboard comparing agent performance on the user's own codebase, meeting/email automation creating tickets from external signals, and Ruby on Rails support. The company's codebase is Ruby on Rails, consistent with the founding team's Rails expertise since 2006.

technologies.label: Multiplayer shared agent session architecture
technologies.summary: The central technology of the talk: a platform architecture enabling one agent session to be simultaneously reachable from Slack, desktop app, GitHub, and mobile with full context preserved across all surfaces. This eliminates the limitation of trapping agents on individual laptops or single interfaces, enabling team-scale collaboration where work can start, continue, and finish from different interfaces. The platform supports multiple coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Factory Droid, Grok Build, Amp, Cursor) and provides collaborative visibility so teammates can see who is involved, ask agents questions in-thread, and view artifacts from any interface. The design principle of model and harness agnosticism (Lesson 0) ensures the platform can switch default models overnight with zero workflow disruption, with open-weight models like GLM-5.2 cited as viable and cheaper alternatives. Over one month of production use, approximately 99.9% of PRs were heavily agent-generated while all remained human-reviewed.
technologies.role: This is the overarching technology framework of the entire talk. Lessons 0 (model agnosticism), 1 (multi-interface shared sessions), and 2 (collaborative visibility) all define aspects of this platform architecture. The talk's title, 'Multiplayer agentic engineering,' directly refers to this technology.

technologies.label: Configurable network sandboxing for agents
technologies.summary: A network sandbox architecture (Lesson 4) that controls which external endpoints coding agents can access, supporting no-access, custom-access (default), and full-access modes. The sandbox prompts for permission before accessing new endpoints, with grants configurable per ticket or project. This enforces least-privilege security by preventing agents from finding production tokens on developer laptops and causing catastrophic damage, and blocks exfiltration of code, secrets, and content. The isolation also enables non-technical team members to safely trigger real engineering work without local development environments. The primary motivation is least-privilege security, not just convenience, because an eager agent told to wipe staging could find a production token on a developer's machine and accidentally delete everything.
technologies.role: Lesson 4 of the talk, covering significant depth on the security rationale, the configurable network sandbox, exfiltration prevention, and the enablement of non-technical team members. The talk's first closing recommendation is to get your codebase working in a sandbox.

technologies.label: Custom codebase-specific agent benchmarking
technologies.summary: A methodology (Lesson 5) for evaluating coding agents by selecting representative pull requests from the team's own repository, replaying them across multiple agent harnesses, and plotting quality against cost and time. This approach is motivated by the observation that public benchmarks like SWE-bench are language-specific (Python, 2,294 instances from 12 Python repositories) and do not reflect a team's actual codebase (Ruby on Rails in this case). The benchmarking produces quality-vs-cost and quality-vs-time scatterplots that inform model selection and enable model-agnostic switching. Results showed Anthropic agents improving in quality but at higher cost and slower speed, while Codex was faster and cheaper, running four times as many sessions. The team switched defaults between Codex and briefly Fiable with no meaningful disruption. The talk also mentions future automatic model routing tailored to the codebase.
technologies.role: Lesson 5 of the talk, with a full benchmark dashboard demo plotting quality vs cost and time across multiple harnesses on their Ruby on Rails codebase. The talk's third closing recommendation is to benchmark to stay model-agnostic and on the frontier of cost, speed, and quality.

technologies.label: Autonomous external signal ingestion into engineering pipelines
technologies.summary: A technique (Lesson 3) for automatically turning external signals—Slack messages, customer calls, Sentry alerts, emails, and meeting conversations—into code and tickets without manual routing. The meeting bot demo shows a bot that sat in a four-hour Google Meet, overheard a suggestion about coding agents needing acceptance criteria, autonomously created a ticket, added acceptance-criteria fields to the product's form, and produced a screenshot on request. The speaker clarifies these are prototypes to evaluate, not final implementations, but every customer call now yields dozens of prototyped ideas and a few shippable PRs. All agent-generated work from external signals remains human-reviewed before merging.
technologies.role: Lesson 3 of the talk, featuring the most detailed demo: a meeting bot that autonomously created tickets and prototyped code changes from overheard conversation. The demo illustrates the broader principle of turning every external signal into code.
